Year A · Term theme: Identity & Belonging
Thread tags: SMSC S/M/So (C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
Identify an adult who can help and communicate a concern clearly.
Owner-approved standalone RSHE outline, 26 October 2026. The approved outline is the weekly source; no separate weekly workbook row is asserted.
A teen needs help. The first adult is away. Who else could help? What could the teen say?
Choose two adults in the story. Show how the teen could ask for help. Choose what to do if help has not come.
RSHE-BUILD-A2-W06-E1: A fictional help-route map, a help request and a follow-up choice, with prompts recorded.

Print both evidence pages and all three support pages. Keep the picture whole. Cut the six story cards and helper choices. The fictional setting has a tutor and a duty adult available in a shared learning area. These are role cards, not names. Prepare a separate adult model and the usual communication aids. Review the local response procedure before teaching. No learner lists real contacts or shares a personal worry.
Year A. Autumn 2 Week 6: 7–11 December 2026. One 40-minute RSHE lesson. No day or clock slot is inferred. This lesson is formative. Week 7 is the assessing lesson.
This helps me raise a concern and find support in learning or work.
Open the title before the timed sequence.
Read the fictional young person’s story.
Read the objective and success checks.
Individual task with the chosen route.
Record actual work, response and support.
Individual exit response and next step.

C uses the second adult route. The person can use speech, a note, signs or an aid; polished words and eye contact are not conditions for help. If the first adult is unavailable, does not listen or the worry remains unresolved, tell another trusted adult. Reteach with the two role cards. If danger is immediate, seek urgent help now and follow the emergency response procedure.

Supported: choose two adult-role cards from the fictional setting, select a request for A, and choose another adult for B or C. Read aloud and record each prompt. Independent: build the route, compose a clear request about A, and explain the next step when the first adult is away or has not helped. Aspire: retain the route, request and follow-up choice. Adapt the request to an aid and explain the difference between an everyday follow-up and urgent help for F.

Use four minutes to make a help route for A: choose a tutor and a duty adult as the second route. Use five minutes to form or select a request that identifies the hidden work and asks for help. Use three minutes to draw B or C and select the next adult. D offers a non-speaking route. All responses remain about the fictional young person.
Read aloud, point, scribe exact words or use the usual communication aid. Record support without treating speech speed or handwriting as the target.

All teaching prompts concern fictional young people. Never ask about a learner’s own body, family or experiences. No touching, personal role-play or real-life comparisons are required. An adult may narrate both fictional parts while the learner chooses or explains a response. Respect a pass, pause or use of an aid without asking why. If a real concern arises, listen calmly and follow the setting’s safeguarding procedure promptly. Do not promise secrecy or use a disclosure as lesson evidence. Safety is the adult’s responsibility; a child is never to blame for another person’s harmful act.

Keep a map or ordered record showing two generic helping-adult roles in the fictional setting. Keep the request about A, including the worry and help sought, in the learner’s chosen mode. Record a follow-up choice for B or C and all prompts. Record what is still missing. A list of adults without a request or follow-up does not meet the full evidence line.

Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // self-edit · ? read back · R responded · E evidence in the evidence record. R requires Voice, Audience, a specific NS+ prompt and the learner response in their own colour. E is recorded only when actual work is banked. Record prompts and unfinished work. Blank sheets and adult models are not completed learner evidence.

Space: calm seating and clear resources. Voice: an optional response about the fictional case. Audience: an adult listens or reads and responds. Influence: record any change to the task support or next teaching step. A pass is respected and does not require an explanation.

S: value a person’s dignity and voice. M: recognise an adult’s responsibility to act on a concern. So: communicate a worry and use support. IL: allow a pass, an aid or another safe route. MR: listen without blame and respect communication needs. No other thread is claimed.
A fictional help request and adult reply may be offered to the Communication portfolio. Keep the learner’s actual words, choice or aid response. Staff confirm any mapping.

A peer keeps hiding a young person’s work. The young person could tell the tutor. The request could say: the teen needs help. A peer keeps hiding the teen’s work. Could the adult help stop this? If help has not come, tell another trusted adult.

C uses the second adult route. The person can use speech, a note, signs or an aid; polished words and eye contact are not conditions for help. If the first adult is unavailable, does not listen or the worry remains unresolved, tell another trusted adult. Reteach with the two role cards. If danger is immediate, seek urgent help now and follow the emergency response procedure.

Record a follow-up choice for B or C and all prompts. Record what is still missing. A list of adults without a request or follow-up does not meet the full evidence line.

The core case is A. B tests an unavailable adult; C tests help that has not yet dealt with the worry. D permits an aid or note. E rejects secrecy about a worry. F needs urgent help, not waiting for the usual lesson or appointment. Use role names only. The lesson is not a list of real contacts and does not ask for home details.

Being older or holding a role does not make every adult safe. The fictional helpers are adults the young person trusts to listen and take action. If an adult is part of the worry, another safe adult can be approached. Keep telling does not mean repeatedly approaching an unsafe adult. A young person does not need proof or perfect words before asking for help.
